zajjaj:109-109.t: His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿وَلَوْ جِئْنا بِمِثْلِهِ مَدَدًا﴾: "مَدَدًا" is accusative as a tamyīz (specification). You say: "لِي مِلْءُ هَذا عَسَلًا" (I have the fill of this in honey) and "مِثْلُ هَذا ذَهَبًا" (the like of this in gold), that is: its like in gold. We have explained the accusative of tamyīz earlier in the book.

zajjaj:110-110.t: His saying: ﴿فَمَن كانَ يَرْجُو لِقاءَ رَبِّهِ﴾: there are two views about it. Some said: its meaning is "whoever fears meeting his Lord", and like it is ﴿ما لَكم لا تَرْجُونَ لِلَّهِ وقارًا﴾ [Nūḥ: 13]; they said its meaning is: "What is the matter with you that you do not fear the majesty of Allah?!" It has also been said: "whoever hopes for a good outcome with his Lord"; and when he hopes for it, he also fears his Lord's punishment. ﴿فَلْيَعْمَلْ عَمَلا صالِحًا﴾: "فَلِيَعْمَلْ" with kasra on the lām is permissible, and it is the original form, but it is heavy in pronunciation and is hardly ever read. If it were begun without the fāʾ, the lām would have kasra; you say: "لِيَعْمَلْ زَيْدٌ بِخَيْرٍ" (let Zayd do good). But when the fāʾ combined with it, and the yāʾ came after the lām, the kasra became heavy with the yāʾ — and it is heavy even on its own. Do you not see that they say "فَخْذٌ" for "فَخِذٌ" (thigh)? [Translator's note: in the first view the text prints "لِقاءُ رَبِّهِ" with ḍamma; the expected case as object of "يَخافُ" is "لِقاءَ".]

zajjaj:10-10.t:
His saying: ﴿إذْ أوى الفِتْيَةُ إلى الكَهْفِ فَقالُوا رَبَّنا آتِنا مِن لَدُنْكَ رَحْمَةً وهَيِّئْ لَنا مِن أمْرِنا رَشَدًا﴾: the meaning of "they took refuge in it" is: they went to it and made it their shelter. "Al-fitya" (the youths) is the plural of "fatā", like "ghulām" and "ghilma", and "ṣabiyy" and "ṣibya". "Fiʿla" is one of the nouns of plurality (asmāʾ al-jamʿ), and it is not a pattern on which analogy may be drawn: "ghurāb" and "ghirba", or "ghaniyy" and "ghinya", are not permissible.

His saying: ﴿فَقالُوا رَبَّنا آتِنا مِن لَدُنْكَ رَحْمَةً﴾, i.e. give us from Yourself mercy, i.e. forgiveness and provision. ﴿وَهَيِّئْ لَنا مِن أمْرِنا رَشَدًا﴾: in "رَشَدًا" the form "rushdan" is permissible, except that it is not read so here, because the verse-endings are on the pattern "faʿal", such as "amad" and "ʿadad"; so "rashad" is better in this place. That is: "guide us to what brings near to You and gains closeness with You".

zajjaj:11-11.t: His saying: ﴿فَضَرَبْنا عَلى آذانِهِمْ في الكَهْفِ سِنِينَ عَدَدًا﴾: the meaning of "We struck upon their ears" is "We prevented them from hearing", because a sleeper who hears wakes up; so the meaning is: "We put them to sleep and prevented them from hearing". "عَدَدًا" is accusative in two ways. One of them is as a maṣdar (verbal noun); the meaning is "We count a counting". It may also be a naʿt (adjective) of "years"; the meaning is "years possessing number". The point of your saying "number" of countable things is that you want to emphasise the large quantity of the thing, because when it is few, its amount and the amount of its number are understood, so it does not need to be counted; and when it is many, it needs to be counted. So "number" in your saying "I stayed days, a number (ayyāman ʿadadan)" means that you intend multitude by it. It is also possible that you emphasise with "number" the meaning of plurality, in that it has gone out of the meaning of the singular.

zajjaj:12-12.t:
The meaning of His saying ﴿ثُمَّ بَعَثْناهُمْ﴾ is: We roused them from their sleep. Everyone who comes out of death into life, or out of sleep into wakefulness, is called "mabʿūth" (raised); and the interpretation of "mabʿūth" is that what was preventing him from acting and rising up has been removed from him.

His saying: ﴿لِنَعْلَمَ أيُّ الحِزْبَيْنِ أحْصى لِما لَبِثُوا أمَدًا﴾: "al-amad" is the extent [of time]. "أمَدًا" is accusative in two ways: it is accusative as a tamyīz (specification); or, if you wish, it is accusative on [the sense of] "أحْصى أمَدًا" (better reckoned the extent), so that the governing word is "أحْصى", as though it were said: "that We may know whether these reckoned the extent better or those". It may also be accusative by "لَبِثُوا", with "أحْصى" attached to "لِما", so that the meaning is: "which of the two parties reckoned better their staying for the extent".

zajjaj:14-14.t:
His saying: ﴿لَقَدْ قُلْنا إذًا شَطَطًا﴾, i.e. "we would then have spoken an injustice". "شَطَطًا" is accusative as a maṣdar (verbal noun); the meaning is: "we would then have spoken a saying of shaṭaṭ (transgression)". One says "shaṭṭa al-rajul" and "ashaṭṭa" when he has acted unjustly. The poet said:
؎ألا يا لَقَوْمِي قَدْ أشَطَّتْ عَواذِلِي ويَزْعُمْنَ أنِّي أقْصَرُ اليَوْمِ باطِلِي
(O my people! My censuring women have gone too far, claiming that my folly has today fallen short.)

zajjaj:15-15.t: His saying: ﴿لَوْلا يَأْتُونَ عَلَيْهِمْ بِسُلْطانٍ بَيِّنٍ﴾: the youths rejected the worship of their people, and that they should worship others besides Allah, so they said: "These, our people, have taken gods besides Him; why do they not bring…". "لَوْلا" is in the meaning of "hallā" (why not); the meaning is: "why do they not bring a clear proof for them?" The meaning of "عَلَيْهِمْ" is: for the worship of the gods.

zajjaj:16-16.t: His saying: ﴿وَإذِ اعْتَزَلْتُمُوهم وما يَعْبُدُونَ إلا اللَّهَ﴾: the position of "ما" is accusative; the meaning is: "when you have withdrawn from them and withdrawn from what they worship except Allah — for you will not abandon worshipping Him". ﴿فَأْوُوا إلى الكَهْفِ﴾, i.e. make the cave your shelter. ﴿يَنْشُرْ لَكم رَبُّكم مِن رَحْمَتِهِ﴾, i.e. He will spread out for you of provision. ﴿وَيُهَيِّئْ لَكم مِن أمْرِكم مِرْفَقًا﴾: one says "it is the mirfaq (elbow) of the arm", with kasra on the mīm and fatḥa on the fāʾ; and likewise "the mirfaq (convenience) of the affair", exactly like the mirfaq of the arm. Al-Aṣmaʿī said: I know nothing other than this. The readers read "مَرْفِقًا", with fatḥa on the mīm and kasra on the fāʾ. Quṭrub and other lexicographers mentioned both forms both in "the marfiq of the affair" and "the mirfaq of the arm", and they all said: "al-mirfaq" for the arm, with kasra on the mīm, is more common in the language and better.

zajjaj:17-17.t:
His saying: ﴿وَتَرى الشَّمْسَ إذا طَلَعَتْ تَزاوَرُ عَنْ كَهْفِهِمْ ذاتَ اليَمِينِ﴾: in "تَزاوَرُ" there are three forms: "تَزاوَرُ"; "تَزْوَرُّ", without alif, on the pattern of "taḥmarru"; and "تَزْوارُّ", on the pattern of "taḥmārru". And a fourth form: "تَزّاوُرُ", whose origin is "tatazāwaru", the tāʾ being assimilated into the zāy. [Translator's note: the text says "three forms" and then adds "a fourth form"; translated as written. The fourth is printed "تَزّاوُرُ", presumably for "tazzāwaru".]

﴿وَإذا غَرَبَتْ تَقْرِضُهم ذاتَ الشِّمالِ﴾: "تَقْرِضُهُمْ", with kasra on the rāʾ, and "تَقْرُضُهُمْ", with ḍamma on the rāʾ; the reading is with the kasra. Its interpretation is: "it turns aside from them and leaves them". Dhū al-Rumma said:
؎إلى ظُعُنٍ يَقْرِضْنَ أقْوازَ مُشْرِفٍ شِمالًا وعَنْ أيْمانِهِنَّ الفَوارِسُ
(Towards women in howdahs who leave the sand-hills of Mushrif on the left, while [the hills of] al-Fawāris are on their right.)
"يَقْرِضْنَ" means: they leave. The root meaning of "al-qarḍ" is cutting, and separating things from one another; from this is your saying "lend me (aqriḍnī) a dirham", whose interpretation is "cut off for me a dirham from your wealth".

His saying: ﴿وَهم في فَجْوَةٍ مِنهُ﴾, i.e. in a wide space of it. ﴿ذَلِكَ مِن آياتِ اللَّهِ﴾: it has been said that the door of the cave faced Banāt Naʿsh (the Great Bear), and for that reason the sun did not rise upon them. This explanation is not clear; rather Allah placed this sign in them because the sun did not come near them at its rising nor at its setting.

His saying: ﴿ذَلِكَ مِن آياتِ اللَّهِ مَن يَهْدِ اللَّهُ فَهو المُهْتَدِ﴾: most usage has "فَهُوَ المُهْتَدِي", retaining the yāʾ, but in the muṣḥaf in this place it is without yāʾ. In this place it is like what is in "al-Aʿrāf", and this is the [correct] way: it is in "al-Aʿrāf" with yāʾ, and in "al-Kahf" without yāʾ. [Translator's note: the text first likens this place to al-Aʿrāf and then says al-Aʿrāf has the yāʾ while al-Kahf does not; translated as written.] Dropping the yāʾ is permissible in nouns specifically and not permissible in verbs, because dropping the yāʾ in a verb is a sign of the jussive (jazm). Dropping the yāʾ occurs in nouns when the noun does not have the alif and lām, such as "muhtadin" and "muqtadin"; then the alif and lām were introduced and the dropping was left as it was, and the kasra indicates the dropped yāʾ.

zajjaj:18-18.t:
His saying: ﴿وَتَحْسَبُهم أيْقاظًا وهم رُقُودٌ﴾: "al-ayqāẓ" are those who are awake, and "al-ruqūd" are those asleep. The singular of ayqāẓ is "yaqiẓ" and "yaqẓān", and the plural is "ayqāẓ". The rajaz poet said:
؎وَوَجَدُوا إخْوَتَهم أيْقاظًا
(And they found their brothers awake.)
It was said in the exegesis that their eyes were open, so that whoever saw them would imagine them to be awake; and it was also said: because of their much turning over, one would think they were not asleep, and what indicates it is ﴿وَنُقَلِّبُهم ذاتَ اليَمِينِ وذاتَ الشِّمالِ﴾. Both "وَتَحْسِبُهُمْ" and "وَتَحْسَبُهُمْ" are permissible. ﴿وَكَلْبُهم باسِطٌ ذِراعَيْهِ بِالوَصِيدِ﴾: "al-waṣīd" is the courtyard of the house, the forecourt of the dwelling.

His saying: ﴿لَوِ اطَّلَعْتَ عَلَيْهِمْ﴾, with kasra on the wāw; it is also read "لَوُ اطَّلَعْتَ عَلَيْهِمْ", with ḍamma on the wāw. The kasra is better, because the wāw is quiescent and the ṭāʾ is quiescent, so the wāw was given kasra because of the meeting of two quiescent letters, and this is the basic rule. The ḍamma is permissible because the ḍamma is of the same kind as the wāw; but when what follows the quiescent letter has a ḍamma, the ḍamma there is better than it is here, as in "أوُ انْقُصْ" and "أوِ انْقُصْ", with ḍamma and with kasra.

His saying: ﴿لَوَلَّيْتَ مِنهم فِرارًا﴾: "فِرارًا" is accusative as a maṣdar (verbal noun), because the meaning of "وَلَّيْتَ" is: you would have fled from them. ﴿وَلَمُلِئْتَ مِنهم رُعْبًا﴾ — also "raʿban", "ruʿuban" — and "رُعْبًا" is accusative as a tamyīz (specification). You say "imtalaʾtu māʾan" (I was filled with water) and "imtalaʾtu faraqan" (I was filled with fear), i.e. "I was filled with fear, and with water". It was said in the exegesis that their hair and their nails had grown very long, and for that reason, if an onlooker saw them, he would flee from them terrified.

zajjaj:19-19.t:
His saying: ﴿فابْعَثُوا أحَدَكم بِوَرِقِكُمْ﴾: there are four forms in it: with fatḥa on the wāw and kasra on the rāʾ; "بِوَرْقِكُمْ", with sukūn on the rāʾ; and "بِوِرْقِكُمْ", with kasra on the wāw and sukūn on the rāʾ. One says "wariq", "warq" and "wirq", as one says "kabid", "kabd" and "kibd" (liver); kasra on the wāw is the weakest of them. "بِوَرِقْكُمْ" is also permissible: you assimilate the qāf into the kāf, so that it becomes a pure kāf.

His saying: ﴿فَلْيَنْظُرْ أيُّها أزْكى طَعامًا﴾: "أيُّها" is nominative as the mubtadaʾ (subject). The meaning of "which of it is purest in food" is: which of its people is purest in food. "أزْكى" is the khabar (predicate) of the mubtadaʾ, and "طَعامًا" is accusative as a tamyīz (specification). It has been said that the interpretation of "purest in food" is "most lawful in food", and they mentioned that most of the people were Magians, and they did not keep their slaughtered animals clean. It has also been said: "purest in food" means "food not taken by usurpation, nor from an unlawful source".

His saying: ﴿فَلْيَأْتِكم بِرِزْقٍ مِنهُ﴾ — and "فَلِيَأْتِكُمْ" — with sukūn on the lām and with kasra; the reading is with sukūn on the lām, and the kasra is permissible. His saying: ﴿وَلا يُشْعِرَنَّ بِكم أحَدًا﴾: it was said: let him not inform anyone about you, i.e. if he is discovered, let him not drag his brothers into what he falls into.
